s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A library management system models the lending of physical copies of titles to members, distinguishing the abstract Book from the concrete BookItem copy, and supporting issue, return, renew, reservation, search, and fine calculation. The core abstractions are Book, BookItem, Member, Librarian, Reservation, and Fine.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India lending out physical gold certificates. The certificate design (Book) is one thing, but each printed copy (BookItem) is a separate physical object with its own status. Rajesh borrows a copy, Priya reserves one that is out, and if Rajesh returns late he pays a fine, exactly like a late fee on a loan.

**One line to remember:** A library lends concrete copies of abstract titles, tracking issue, return, renewal, reservation, and fines.

sections.s2_technical:
The key modelling insight is the separation of `Book` (title, author, ISBN) from `BookItem` (a physical copy with a barcode and status). One book has many book items, which is a one-to-many composition. A `Member` can hold several issued items up to a limit.

Issuing finds a free `BookItem`, marks it ISSUED, and records a due date. Returning marks it AVAILABLE and, if overdue, computes a `Fine` through a fine policy. Renewal extends the due date only if no one has reserved the title. Reservation lets a member queue for a title whose copies are all out; when a copy returns, the first reservation is notified.

```java
librarian.issue(member, "978-0134685991");
```

Search is served by indexes keyed on title, author, and ISBN so lookups are fast. The senior nuance is concurrency: two members returning and reserving the same title simultaneously must be serialized so a copy is not double-issued, which I handle with per-title locking.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India staff library stocks multiple copies of a compliance handbook. Rajesh wants to borrow one copy while another is already out. The system must find an available copy and track its due date. This is exactly the Book-versus-BookItem separation and the issue flow.

Problem 2 — Rajesh returns the book three days late, so a fine must be charged accurately in rupees. This is exactly the fine-policy logic.

The code defines `Book`, `BookItem`, `Member`, a `FinePolicy`, and a `Librarian` service handling issue and return, with a demo where Rajesh borrows and returns late.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: one copy BC-1 of the handbook, Rajesh issues it on 1 October with a 14-day loan, returns on 18 October.

Step 1: `issue` scans copies, finds BC-1 AVAILABLE, marks it ISSUED to Rajesh, and sets the due date to 15 October. Step 2: the item appears in Rajesh's issued list. Step 3: `returnItem` on 18 October computes overdue days as 18 minus 15 equals 3. Step 4: the copy becomes AVAILABLE again and `PerDayFine` charges 3 times 10 equals 30 rupees.

```
Oct 31 22:09 INFO LIB: Rajesh issued Banking Compliance Handbook due 2026-10-15
Oct 31 22:09 INFO LIB: Rajesh returned; overdue=3 fine=30
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh ─▶ Librarian.issue(handbook)
     │ find AVAILABLE copy BC-1 → ISSUED, due=+14d
     ▼
  Member.issued = [BC-1]
     │ ... returns 3 days late ...
     ▼
  Librarian.returnItem(BC-1)
     │ copy → AVAILABLE, overdue=3
     │ FinePolicy.fine(3) → 30
     ▼
  charge 30
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design a library management system, the single most important modelling decision is separating the Book from the BookItem. A Book is the abstract title with its ISBN, author, and name, while a BookItem is one physical copy with its own barcode, status, and due date. A book has many items, so when a member borrows, I am lending a specific copy, not the abstract title, and this separation is what makes multi-copy lending correct.

The main actors are the Member who borrows, holds a limited number of items, and can reserve titles, and the Librarian service that performs issue, return, and renewal. Issuing finds an available copy, marks it issued, and stamps a due date. Returning frees the copy and, if it is overdue, charges a fine. Renewal extends the due date, but only when no one has reserved the title, so a waiting member is never blocked.

I pull fine calculation into a fine policy interface so the library can move from a flat per-day fine to a tiered one without touching the lending logic, which is the Open/Closed principle. Reservations use an observer-style notification: when a copy returns, the first member in the reservation queue is notified that their copy is ready. Search is backed by indexes on title, author, and ISBN so lookups are fast.

The concurrency concern I always call out is that two members acting on the same title at the same instant must be serialized, otherwise a single copy could be issued twice. I handle that with per-title locking. In my banking work at National Bank of India, this is the same discipline I apply to lending any limited physical asset — distinguishing the design from the instance, tracking status transitions precisely, and charging late fees through a replaceable policy.
